question_short_text: Why does per capita income grow faster at current prices than at constant prices?

explanation: Per capita income at constant prices adjusts for inflation (increase in price level). This removes the purely nominal gain and shows real purchasing power growth. Per capita income at current prices reflects both real growth and the inflation effect, making it appear higher.

research.summary: The distinction between nominal (current price) and real (constant price) per capita income measures is fundamental to understanding economic growth. When we measure per capita income at current prices without any inflation adjustment, the figure includes both genuine increases in productive output and the mechanical effect of rising price levels. Constant prices, by contrast, hold the reference year's price levels fixed, allowing us to see what the actual growth in purchasing power has been. India's nominal GDP per capita grew at an average 10.9% annually over the last decade while real GDP per capita at constant 2011-12 prices grew at 5.6% per year—the difference of approximately 5.3 percentage points represents primarily the inflation component. The question specifically tests whether a student understands that per capita income growth appears inflated when measured at current prices because inflation mechanically increases the money value of every unit of output, even if the quantity produced or its real value remains unchanged. The trap is that students often confuse this with population growth (which affects the denominator) or money supply growth (which is a separate monetary phenomenon). The core insight is that inflation rate is the key driver of the gap: if prices rise by 5% while real output per person grows only 2%, the nominal figure will show 7% growth, misleading policymakers who do not adjust for price effects. This is why all serious economic comparisons over time use constant-price measures as the standard.
facts: In nominal terms, India's nominal GDP per capita reached ₹234,859 in 2024-25 compared to ₹215,936 in 2023-24, while at constant 2011-12 prices it stood at ₹133,501, showing the magnitude of the nominal-real gap.
The difference between nominal and real growth rates is a primary measure of inflation in the economy; sustained inflation narrows the gap between the two measures.
Per capita income measures are derived by dividing total national income (GDP or NNI) by mid-year population; thus population growth affects both measures equally, making option (a) incorrect.

Nominal per capita income figures are susceptible to currency fluctuations in international comparisons, which is why PPP-adjusted measures are preferred for cross-country living standard comparisons.
